# Controlled rolling of steel plate and strip

The major purpose of controlled rolling is to refine grain structure and, thereby, to enhance both the strength and toughness of steel in the as-hot-rolled condition. If a survey is made of the development of controlled rolling, it can be seen that controlled rolling consists of three stage: (a) deformation in the recrystallization region at high temperature; (b) deformation in the non-recrystallization region within a low temperature range above Ar3; and (c) deformation in the austenite-ferrite region. It is stressed that the importance of deformation in the non-recrystallization region is in dividing an austenite grain into several block by the introduction of deformation band within it. Deformation in the austenite-ferrite region gives a mixed structure consisting of equiaxed grain and subgrain after transformation and, thereby, it increases further the strength and toughness. The fundamental difference between conventionally hot-rolled and controlled-rolled steel lies in the fact that the nucleation of ferrite occurs exclusively at austenite grain boundary in the former, while it occurs in the grain interior as well as at grain boundary in the latter, leading to a more refined grain structure. In controlled-rolled steel a crystallographic texture develops, which causes planar anisotropy in mechanical property and embrittlement in the through-thickness direction. The latter is shown to be the main cause of the delamination which appeared in the fractured Charpy specimen. Fundamental aspect of controlled rolling, such as the recrystallization behaviour of austenite, the retardation mechanism of austenite recrystallization due to niobium, microstructural change accompanying deformation, factor governing strength and toughness, etc., are reviewed. The practice of controlled rolling in plate and strip mill is outlined.

## HISTORICAL SURVEY

Controlled rolling is a means of improving the property of steel in the hot-rolled condition to a level equivalent to, or greater than those of highly alloyed or heat-treated steel. Modern controlled rolling has been practised on numerous mill and laboratory experiment which have been performed to obtain high strength, good toughness, and good weldability. The basic idea is to control the rolling process in order to refine the austenite structure, and thereby to give fine ferrite grain.

In 1924 Arrowsmith had already pointed out the advantage of grain refinement. It has been known for many year that improvement in mechanical property result when structural steel are rolled to low finishing temperature. Hanemann and Lucke interpreted this in term of recrystallization after hot deformation with the α-grain (ferrite grain) size being reduced with decreasing deformation temperature in the γ-region (austenite region). In 1947 Barr and Tipper showed that in mild steel plate the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature was raised by an increase in α-grain size. Examining as-rolled plate, Mackenzie showed a correlation between transition temperature and finish-rolling temperature, a factor affecting γ-grain size. Similar result have been reported by other investigator. The above report have one factor in common: hot rolling was carried out as usual at high temperature, and only the last one or two pass were rolled at a lower temperature. Therefore, the result obtained were not always definite, and were in disagreement with each other.

After World War 2, in order to prevent the occurrence of brittle fracture, notch toughness was required in shipbuilding and in other structural steel plate. In general, the refinement of microstructure by Al (aluminium) killing, normalizing, and an increase in the ratio of manganese to carbon content were adopted to meet the requirement for notch toughness. Instead of normalizing, however, controlled low-temperature hot rolling was being practised by some mill in Europe to provide increased notch toughness in hot-rolled plate. The practice involved making the last few hot-rolling pass at temperature lower than normal. The optimum temperature for the last pass was just above the Ar3 temperature. This rolling schedule was fairly similar to the present controlled rolling and its prototype.

In 1959, Beiser reported that the small addition of Nb (niobium) caused a large increase in strength but reduced notch toughness markedly in as-hot-rolled steel plate. It was Great Lakes Steel, which produced as-hot-rolled high-strength Nb-bearing steel for the first time in 1960. In order to prevent a deterioration in notch toughness, the application of controlled rolling to Nb-bearing steel was studied. According to Norén's review:

(i) when hot rolled under conventional rolling condition, Nb steel deteriorated markedly in toughness; (ii) when finish rolled at lower temperature, the improvement in toughness was much greater for Nb steel than for Nb-free steel; and (iii) when finish rolled below 800 °C, or when total reduction below 900 °C was more than 30%, notch toughness improved remarkably. The strength increase resulting from the addition of Nb was found to be due to precipitation hardening of fine Nb(C, N) which formed in the α-matrix during cooling. In order to make full use of precipitation hardening, Nb(C, N) had to be dissolved at a high temperature before hot rolling, which coarsened the γ-grain structure. When coarse γ was hot rolled conventionally, the transformed structure was a mixture consisting of coarse α and bainite, thereby deteriorating notch toughness. Using these method, the basis of combining controlled rolling with Nb steel was established.

Research on controlled rolling was carried out by the BISRA group in the 1960s, which opened the way for the development of the present controlled-rolling technology. It is difficult to pinpoint the beginning, but the development of C—Mn (manganese)—Nb fine-grained steel commenced about 1958. Duckworth et al. showed that with the C content below 0.1%, and by using Nb addition and a low finishing temperature with heavy draughting, very attractive property could be obtained in the as-rolled condition. Pearlite-free steel and pearlite-reduced steel proposed by Duckworth et al. were intended to improve weldability and toughness by reducing the C content, to increase strength by addition of Nb and/or V, and to improve toughness by using a low finishing temperature. It was Phillips and Chapman, Irani et al. and Jones and Rothwell who, for the first time, turned their attention to controlled rolling itself. They showed that Nb retarded recrystallization greatly, thereby enabling the deformation of γ (austenite) in the non-recrystallization region, that transformation from deformed γ produced a fine α-grain (ferrite grain) structure, and that an improper draught schedule tended to cause a mixed grain structure. However, because their experiment were carried out in a laboratory bar mill, and the only measure of controlled rolling was the finishing temperature, their result lacked generality.

Research on controlled rolling motivated by the BISRA group has been undertaken very actively, including fundamental and applied aspect. Fundamental aspect include item such as the recrystallization behaviour of γ the retardation mechanism of recrystallization due to Nb, microstructural change accompanying deformation in the non-recrystallization γ-region and its influence on transformation behaviour, and factor governing grain structure after transformation.

Through these investigation, the importance of deformation in the non-recrystallization region was recognized. It was also made clear that controlled rolling was not to cease in the γ-region, but was to be extended into the γ–α-region (austenite–ferrite region), thereby enhancing both strength and toughness. Modern controlled rolling means the overall technology consisting of (i) a suitable selection of chemical composition, (ii) a proper slab-reheating temperature to obtain small and uniform γ-grain, (iii) γ-grain refinement owing to repeated deformation recrystallization, (iv) deformation in the non-recrystallization region, (v) deformation in the γ–α two-phase region, and (vi) controlled cooling.

The full-scale production of controlled-rolled plate and hot-rolled strip commenced with the construction of large-diameter pipeline, which required high-strength steel with good toughness and weldability. In fact, pipeline applied to Arctic-temperature service were impossible to construct without controlled-rolled plate.

Finally, the great contribution from Hall and Petch must be recognized. The Hall-Petch relation correlates yield stress with ferrite grain size. Heslop and Petch also associated transition temperature with grain size; they guided the development of controlled rolling throughout its whole course.

## FUNDAMENTAL OF CONTROLLED ROLLING

The major purpose of controlled rolling is to refine the structure of steel and, thereby, to enhance both strength and toughness. Because of the relation between γ– and α-grain size, refinement of the α-structure is achieved mainly through γ-grain refinement. The change in grain structure with deformation temperature has been studied by many investigator. Many study were confined to deformation in the γ-region alone, while few of them were extended to deformation in the γ–α two-phase region.

Kozasu et al. divided deformation temperature in the γ-region into three range in association with the change in γ- and α-grain structure. Deformation above 1000 °C brings about coarse, recrystallized γ-grain, which transform to a relatively coarse α and upper bainitic structure (range 1). Deformation in the intermediate temperature range from 1000 °C to 900 °C refine γ (austenite) by repeated recrystallization, leading to fine-grained α (range 2). Deformation below the recrystallization temperature produces 'warm-worked' γ, which leads to a finer α-grain (ferrite grain) structure (range 3). The grain refinement is achieved mainly by deformation in range 2 and 3. The transition temperature was shown to decrease in a linear manner with an increase in total reduction in range 2 and 3.

From a practical viewpoint, Baird and Preston proposed a similar but slightly different interpretation. Figure 1 depicts the rolling procedure involving reduction in the rapid-recrystallization region (range 1), delay in rolling (in range 2), and final reduction in the non-recrystallization region (range 3). Delay in rolling is a necessary procedure for ensuring the required amount of deformation in the non-recrystallization region. During the delay, however, partial recrystallization tends to occur, thereby leading to the formation of a mixed grain structure.

1 Schematic representation of various process taking place during controlled rolling of C—Mn (manganese)—Nb (niobium) steel; after Baird and Preston

According to Fukuda et al., there are two type of austenite-to-ferrite transformation mode during hot rolling, shown in Fig. 2. Type 1 is the transformation from recrystallized γ to α, where α nucleation takes place exclusively at recrystallized γ-grain boundary. Type 1 is subdivided into two, A and B: type 1A and 1B are equivalent to range 1 and 2 above, respectively. Rolling passes at high temperature do not contribute to the refinement of the γ-grain structure ( γ-grain size $\lesssim$ ASTM 5), which transforms to a coarse α and/or Widmanstätten-like structure (type 1A). Deformation at low temperature in the recrystallization region produces a fine-grained γ-structure ( γ-grain size $\gtrsim$ ASTM 6), which transforms to a fine-grained ferrite–pearlite structure (type 1B). Type 2 is the transformation mode from unrecrystallized γ to α, where α nucleation occurs at grain interior as well as at grain boundary, and whereby ultra-fine α-grain are obtained. The transition type is in the intermediate mode between type 1 and 2, giving a mixed grain structure. When a comparison is made, the finest α-grain is obtained by type 2, followed by type 1B, transition type, and type 1A. However, α-grain structure is more homogeneous for type 1B than for type 2.

2 Schematic diagram of type of austenite-to-ferrite transformation for hot-worked steel; after Fukuda et al.

3 Effect of recrystallized austenite grain size and total reduction in non-recrystallization region on a ferrite grain size and b upper bainite fraction in Mn-Nb-V steel; after Sekine and Maruyama

Sekine and Maruyama showed that α-grain structure is decided by the recrystallized γ-grain size before deformation in the non-recrystallization region and the amount of deformation in that region. Figure 3 depicts the effect of total reduction in the non-recrystallization region on α-grain size (Fig. 3a) and upper bainite volume fraction (Fig. 3b). When a recrystallized γ-grain (austenite grain) size is large, it is difficult to suppress the formation of upper bainite even by large deformation. However, when the recrystallized grain size is small, upper bainite is not allowed to form, even with moderate deformation, giving fine-grained α (ferrite). Sekine and Maruyama emphasized that the best way is to refine γ through recrystallization as much as possible (type 1B), followed by deformation in the non-recrystallization region (type 2) and whereby a uniform, fine-grained α-structure is produced.

The difference between Fukuda et al. and Sekine and Maruyama is that the former stressed type 2 to achieve a fine-grained α-structure, whereas the latter emphasized the importance of the combination of type 1B and 2. This argument is, however, reduced to the uniformity of α nucleation within unrecrystallized γ-grain which, in turn, is reduced to the uniformity in deformation-band density throughout unrecrystallized grain, since α nucleate on deformation band as well as at γ-grain boundary. There has been some evidence that deformation-band density has the propensity to be heterogeneous and that not all the deformation band have the same ferrite-nucleating potential, suggesting that type 2 tends to produce a mixed α-grain structure compared with the optimum combination of type 1B and 2.

So far, controlled rolling has been confined to deformation in the γ-region. Coleman et al. and Gladman and Dulieu obtained a further increase in strength by extending deformation into the γ + α (austenite + ferrite) and/or α-region, and by developing a substructure. Advancing this idea, Tanaka et al. proposed the three stage of the controlled-rolling process: (i) deformation in the γ-recrystallization region, (ii) deformation in the non-recrystallization region, and (iii) deformation in the γ–α (austenite–ferrite) two-phase region.

Figure 4 illustrates schematically the three stage of the controlled-rolling process, and the microstructural change accompanying deformation in each stage. Stage 1: coarse austenite $a$ is refined by repeated deformation and recrystallization $b$, but still transforms to relatively coarse ferrite $b'$; stage 2: deformation band are formed in elongated, unrecrystallized austenite $c$, and ferrite nucleate on the deformation band as well as γ-grain boundary, giving fine α $c'$; stage 3: deformation in the γ–α two-phase region continues stage 2 and also deforms the ferrite, producing a substructure $d$. During cooling after deformation, unrecrystallized austenite transforms to equiaxed α-grain, while deformed ferrite change into subgrain $d'$.

4 Schematic illustration of three stage of controlled-rolling process and change in microstructure with deformation in each stage; after Tanaka

Grain refinement through repeated recrystallization does not proceed indefinitely but reaches a certain limiting value $b$ and thereby results in relatively coarse α-grain $b'$. A mean of breaking the limiting value is to divide the γ-grain. Since a recrystallized γ-grain (austenite grain) $b$ is divided by deformation band $c$, the final α-grain structure is much smaller for $c'$ than for $b'$. The deformation in the two-phase region causes further grain refinement and a mixed structure consisting of equiaxed grain and subgrain. Additional strengthening is obtained by subgrain hardening.

The fundamental difference between conventional hot rolling and controlled rolling lie in that, in the former, α (ferrite) nucleates exclusively at γ-grain boundary, whereas in the latter α nucleation occurs at grain interior as well as grain boundary, which leads to a large difference in the final α-grain structure between the two. The fact that the deformation band is equivalent to the γ-grain boundary with regard to ferrite-nucleating potentiality, means that a γ-grain is divided into several block by deformation band. A comparison between conventional hot rolling and controlled rolling is very similar to that between normalizing and quenching. In conventionally hot-rolled and normalized steel, α nucleates exclusively at γ-grain boundary, which limits grain refinement, whereas in controlled-rolled and quenched steel, the γ-grain is divided into several block; the former is by deformation band and the latter by martensitic transformation, producing a much finer grain structure.

Since unrecrystallized γ containing deformation band promotes the γ to α transformation, from a different viewpoint, controlled rolling can be defined as a process for accelerating α transformation and thereby for producing fine-grained α in steel with medium hardenability which, without being controlled rolled, will transform to a bainitic structure, giving poor toughness.

The effect of each stage deformation on microstructure and mechanical property is described below.

## DEFORMATION IN RECRYSTALLIZATION REGION

## Dynamic recrystallization

There are two kind of restoration process associated with hot working, dynamic and static. When steel is deformed in the austenitic state at high temperature, the flow stress rises to a maximum and then falls to a steady state, see Fig. 5a. In a range of strain less than that for the peak stress dynamic recovery operates, while in the steady-state region dynamic recrystallization occurs. The structure developed by dynamic restoration are thermodynamically unstable, and when held at temperature they are modified by the static-restoration process. Three static-restoration process can be operative, static recovery, static recrystallization, and metadynamic (post-dynamic) recrystallization, see Fig. 5b.

5 Schematic representation of $a$ stress-strain curve and $b$ of inter-relation between three softening mechanism and of dependence on strain of softening proportion attributable to each mechanism; hatched area is forbidden zone; after Djaic and Jonas

The dynamically recrystallized grain size d is associated with the Zener–Hollomon parameter Z, which is a temperature-compensated strain rate, and is given by the following equation:

$$
d ^ {- 1} \propto \sigma_ {\mathrm{flow}} \propto \log Z \tag{1}
$$

$$
Z = \dot {\epsilon} \exp \left(Q _ {\mathrm{dif}} / R T\right) \tag{2}
$$

where $\dot{\epsilon}$ is the strain rate, $Q_{\mathrm{dif}}$ is the activation energy for the self-diffusion of iron, $R$ is the gas constant, and $T$ is absolute temperature. This relation was found to exist for Nb (niobium) steel hot rolled under a certain condition, shown in Fig. 6. However, since a critical strain for the onset of steady state is very large, even at high temperature, it is almost impossible to hot roll steel, and in particular Nb steel, in the steady-state region. This means, in turn, that it is almost impossible to refine the γ-grain (austenite grain) through dynamic recrystallization. Instead, grain refinement must be achieved by static recrystallization.

6 Relation between Zener—Hollomon parameter and reciprocal of recrystallized austenite grain size in Nb steel; after Sekine and Maruyama

## Static recrystallization

Static recrystallization accompanying hot deformation proceed in a similar manner to that in cold-worked material. Nucleation site for new grain are predominantly triple junction of grain and grain boundary, and nucleation within grain is almost nil. The distribution of nucleus is highly localized and inhomogeneous; while some grain boundary give rise to numerous nucleus, there are boundary where nucleus are completely absent. The progress of recrystallization after nucleation is essentially the migration of the recrystallizing front into deformed matrix as is usual in recrystallization. The completion of recrystallization is followed by normal grain growth.

Effect of the amount of deformation and deformation temperature on recrystallized grain size are shown in Fig.7. The recrystallized grain size decreases rapidly as the amount of reduction increase, reaching a limiting value. The limiting grain size decreases with reducing initial grain size. Although a lower deformation temperature produces smaller grain size, the effect of temperature is slight. Figure 8 depicts γ-grain refinement in C–Mn (manganese) and C–Mn–Nb steel during continuous rolling, and it is seen that the grain size decreases from ASTM No.—2 to 7 during rolling over the temperature range 1250–850 °C.

7 Influence of amount of single-pass deformation and deformation temperature on recrystallized austenite grain size in plain C and Nb steel; after Tanaka et al.

Since nucleation site for recrystallization are predominantly at the grain boundary, the initial grain size plays an important role in determining recrystallized grain size. Ouchi et al. showed that recrystallized grain size decreases in a linear manner with the product of strain and total grain-boundary area. Using stainless steel, Towle and Gladman showed that recrystallized grain size $d_{rex}$ can be expressed by

$$
d _ {\mathrm{rex}} = k \epsilon^ {- 0.5} d _ {0} Z ^ {- 0.06} \quad , \tag{3}
$$

where $k$ is a constant, $\epsilon$ is the amount of strain, $d_0$ is the initial grain size, and $Z$ is the Zener-Hollomon parameter. Equation (3) also indicates the slight effect of strain rate on recrystallized grain size.

Variation in recrystallized austenite grain size with rolling pass in plain C and Nb steel; steel were quenched following hot rolling; after Sekine and Maruyama

9 Effects of deformation temperature and initial grain size on critical amount of deformation required for completion of recrystallization in plain C and Nb (niobium) steel; after Tanaka et al.

## Condition for recrystallization

Taking static recrystallization after hot deformation as a prerequisite condition, the effect of various factor on recrystallized grain size have been described so far. It must be stressed, however, that static recrystallization accompanying hot deformation does not occur under all condition.

10 Austenite recrystallization and resulting grain size as function of rolling temperature and reduction for 0.03%Nb steel; steel was reheated to 1250 °C for 20 min, rolled with one pass, and quenched; initial grain-size number was 1.0; after Ouchi et al.

On the contrary, it is necessary to apply more deformation than that required for recrystallization. The critical amount of deformation, $R_{crit}$ , required for the completion of recrystallization is small, as is the temperature dependence in plain C steel. In Nb steel, however, $R_{crit}$ is very large and its temperature dependence substantially higher. The effect of deformation temperature and initial grain size on $R_{crit}$ are shown in Fig. 9. In Nb steel, the effect of grain size on $R_{crit}$ is extremely large, and $R_{crit}$ increases rapidly with decreasing deformation temperature. Recrystallization is virtually suppressed below 950 °C.

Ouchi et al. and Tanaka et al. studied the general recrystallization behaviour by single-pass rolling, shown in Fig. 10. Recrystallization behaviour is divided into three region, recovery, partial recrystallization, and recrystallization. The recrystallization region is subdivided into static and dynamic. The critical amount of deformation dividing each region increases rapidly with decreasing deformation temperature. It is also influenced markedly by the addition of microalloying element, and in particular Nb. Reduction in the recrystallization region produces a fine, uniform recrystallized grain structure. Reduction in the partial-recrystallization region produces a mixed structure consisting of recrystallized grain and recovered grain. Reduction in the recovery region produces locally very coarse grain due to strain-induced grain-boundary migration, while most grain remain unchanged, releasing stored energy by recovery, As is clear from Fig. 10, it is very difficult to roll steel in the recrystallization region and, in particular, during the initial pass in the plate mill, since $R_{\text{crit}}$ is extremely large. In practice, rolling pass are carried out in the recovery region or, at most, in the partial-recrystallization region. Tanaka et al. described clearly how to achieve grain refinement and how to obtain a uniform grain structure under these condition. Even if deformation is applied repeatedly in the recovery region, very sluggish and incomplete recrystallization occurs, while huge grain larger than the initial size are produced locally and persist throughout rolling, see Fig. 11, which leads to the formation of a mixed α-grain (ferrite grain) structure. However, if reduction is applied in the partial-recrystallization region, recrystallization increase in volume fraction with an increasing number of pass, reaching complete recrystallization, see Fig. 12. However, once huge grain are formed by a slight reduction in the recovery region, they persist even after many pass in the partial-recrystallization region. In summarizing the above description, if the initial rolling pass are made in the recovery region, huge grain are formed locally, owing to the strain-induced grain-boundary migration, which persist throughout the whole course of rolling. They transform to upper bainite and/or coarse ferrite grain, giving poor toughness. On the other hand, if a reduction per pass greater than that for partial recrystallization is given successively, a uniform and refined grain structure is obtained. Once complete recrystallization takes place, successive recrystallization proceeds much more easily.

It is considered that the strain-induced precipitation of fine Nb(C, N) is the reason that the critical amount of reduction required for recrystallization and its temperature dependence is much larger for Nb (niobium) steel than for plain C steel.

## Formation of mixed grain structure

Controlled rolling produces a finer α-grain size than not only conventional hot rolling but normalizing. Unfortunately, controlled-rolled steel often exhibits a mixed structure consisting of fine and coarse α-grain and/or upper bainite, decreasing low-temperature toughness.

Mixed grain structure of α is attributed to that of γ (austenite) . Under the circumstance where partial recrystallization occurs, fine recrystallized grain tend to form at γ-grain boundary, leaving an unrecrystallized region in the grain interior where the mixed γ-grain structure is produced. When γ-grain are coarse, or when rapid grain growth takes place after recrystallization owing to an unsuitable deformation condition, a mixed γ-grain structure tends to be induced. Once a mixed γ-grain structure occurs, it cannot be eliminated by later rolling pass. This is considered due to the fact that, when rolled again, the recrystallized region in the vicinity of grain boundary in the previous pass tends to recrystallize preferentially, since it has a smaller grain size than the unrecrystallized region of the grain interior (see Fig. 9). To prevent the formation of a mixed grain structure, suitable condition of holding or a 'continuous' schedule involving reduction in the whole temperature range have been proposed (see Fig. 1). The formation and prevention of a mixed grain structure at high temperature have already been described in the previous section.

## DEFORMATION IN NON-RECRYSTALLIZATION REGION

## Retardation of recrystallization

In order to decrease grain size further, deformation in the non-recrystallization region must be applied following deformation in the recrystallization region.

13 Recrystallization of austenite following single deformation of 50% in various steel; after Irvine et al.

In plain C steel, recrystallization becomes sluggish at low temperature in the γ-region (about 900 °C ≈ Ar3 ). Nb has a powerful influence in retarding γ-recrystallization, thereby achieving a non-recrystallized state, see Figs. 13 and 14. They show a marked temperature dependence of the progress of recrystallization, and also a large recrystallization-retarding effect of Nb. Kozasu et al. reported that, besides a very large retarding effect of Nb, V had some retarding effect, while Al (aluminium) and Al+N accelerated recrystallization slightly. Although both V and Nb are strong carbide-forming element the former does not have any retarding effect, while the latter exhibits a very strong retarding effect. This is considered due to difference in solubility in γ , and strain-induced precipitation potential between the two element. The retardation of recrystallization due to Nb (niobium) can be exhibited only when Nb is in solution in γ before deformation. If Nb remains undissolved because of a low heating temperature, it does not demonstrate any delaying effect.

14 Fraction recrystallized in austenite as function of holding time in plain C and Nb steel; steel were reheated to 1250 °C, hot rolled to 30%, and held at rolling temperature; after Ohmori

The recrystallization retardation due to Nb has been discussed by many investigator. It has been attributed to (i) a solute-drag effect, (ii) strain-induced precipitation of fine Nb(C,N), or (iii) the combined effect of solute Nb and precipitation of fine Nb(C,N). Coladas et al. reported that the main influence of Nb alloying is on the incubation time for the start of recrystallization, and not on the kinetic of recrystallization after incubation and, further, that the delayed recrystallization is due to a solute effect, see Fig. 15.

15 Dependence of time constant in Avrami's law on temperature; $X = 1 - \exp[-(t/\tau)^n]$, where $X$ is fraction recrystallized, $t$ is time, $\tau$ is time constant, and $n$ is constant; after Coladas et al.

16 Time—temperature—precipitation diagram showing effect of deformation of Nb(C, N) in austenite in Nb steel which was reheated to 1260 °C, grain refined, and deformed to 30%; after Watanabe et al.

The retarding effect due to the strain-induced precipitation of fine Nb(C, N) has been proposed by many investigator using several different approach. Ohmori suggested a retarding effect due to fine precipitation, based on the fact that the relation between time for recrystallization and the reciprocal of temperature does not obey a linear relation, which is well explained in term of the concurrent precipitation of Nb(C, N). Jones and Rothwell and other observed the precipitation of Nb(C, N) on the deformation substructure of γ (austenite), which retarded subsequent recrystallization. By holding isothermally after hot deformation, Watanabe et al. observed the progress of the precipitation of Nb(C, N), which was determined by the electrolytic-extraction technique, see Fig. 16. The start of precipitation is accelerated markedly by deformation, suggesting interaction between the precipitate and retardation of recrystallization.

Jonas and Weiss reported that the addition of Nb to γ retard recrystallization in two distinct way; that there is a significant delay introduced by a solute effect, and that under condition where precipitation is more rapid than solute-retarded recrystallization, operation of the recrystallization process is prevented or retarded until precipitation is complete or nearly complete. Combining their result with that of le Bon et al., Jonas and Weiss constructed a recrystallization—precipitation—time (RPT) diagram, shown in Fig. 17. When the time for the start of precipitation $P_{S}$ is longer than the recrystallization start time $R_{S}$, the RPT (recrystallization–precipitation–time) curve has the normal dependence on temperature affected by a solute drag. When $P_{S}$ is less than $R_{S}$, the nucleation and growth of recrystallization is severely impeded.

## Formation of deformation band

Figure 18 shows an elongated γ-grain structure produced by deformation in the γ-region (Fig. 18a) and partially transformed grain structure (Fig. 18b). α-grain (ferrite grain) are nucleated in deformation band as well as γ-grain boundary, individual grain being formed frequently within γ-grain. Although the nature of deformation band is not known exactly, they generally exist in closely packed pair of parallel line which often terminate within a grain, creating a twin-like pattern in heterogeneous distribution. The study on deformation band are not numerous. As shown in Fig. 19, deformation-band density increases a little in the strain range of less than $30\%$, beyond which it increases rapidly with increasing reduction. The deformation-band density is barely affected by deformation temperature in the non-recrystallization region, but it decreases rapidly when the temperature exceeds ~1000 °C while according to Sekine and Maruyama the apparent γ-grain-boundary area (γ-grain boundary plus deformation band) increases with an increasing amount of reduction, reaching a steady level above $\sim 30\%$ reduction. It is worth noting that, with an increasing amount of reduction, the γ-grain-boundary area increases gradually, while deformation-band density increases rapidly, indicating that α-grain refinement resulting from deformation in the non-recrystallization region is due mainly to an increase in the deformation band. The grain-boundary area is increased only by a factor of about 2 when total deformation in the non-recrystallization region is 70–80%. It is also important to note that even when the deformation band is saturated in number, about 10% of γ-grain contain very few deformation band, and that not all deformation band have the same ferrite-nucleation potential; some band only have very thin, straight band of α , implying poor nucleation capacity. Even the introduction of deformation band cannot bring about uniform and homogeneous γ-grain (austenite grain) structure and thereby homogeneous α-grain structure. Inhomogeneity in grain structure is the fate of as-hot-rolled material which can, however, be reduced with a decrease in recrystallized γ-grain size before deformation in the non-recrystallization region.

## DEFORMATION IN AUSTENITE—FERRITE REGION

## Change in microstructure and mechanical property

A limiting γ-grain (austenite grain) size achieved by deformation in the recrystallization region is broken by deformation in the non-recrystallization region. Grain refinement due to deformation in the non-recrystallization region reaches a limiting value at 60–70% reduction. This limit can be broken only by deformation in the γ–α (austenite–ferrite) two-phase region. Besides grain refinement, deformation in the two-phase region gives a substantially different effect on microstructure and mechanical property. Microstructural change accompanying deformation in the two-phase region has already been shown schematically in Fig.4. Figure 21 shows the change in intensity of the (200) reflection, strength, and toughness with deformation in the two-phase region. With an increasing amount of deformation, the yield and tensile strength increase, while the transition temperature and absorbed energy decrease. Microstructural change accompanying deformation in the two-phase region is shown in Fig.22. Deformation in the γ-region alone produces a microstructure consisting of equiaxed α-grain (ferrite grain) with low dislocation density (see Fig.22a and b). Deformation in the two-phase region produces a mixed grain structure, which consists of equiaxed α-grain and 'cold-worked' grain in term of an optical microscopic scale, or consists of polygonal grain and subgrain in term of an electron microscopic scale (see Fig. 22c and d). The deformed γ transforms to polygonal α, while the deformed α change into subgrain. In deformed α, recrystallization is very sluggish, producing subgrain. This is because of the stabilization of the α sub-boundary network due to strain-induced precipitation of Nb(C, N) and/or V(C, N). It is postulated that, during rolling, the γ to α transformation can nucleate on the unrecovered dislocation substructure. Thus, formed α-grain soon impinge on existing γ-subgrain and cannot grow further. This kind of mutual interaction between deformed γ and α produces a further decrease in α-grain size.

Deformation in the two-phase region produces a duplex structure consisting of soft polygonal grain and hard subgrain. On the other hand, deformation of γ produces a single structure consisting of soft grain alone. This difference in microstructure between the two controlled-rolling condition brings about a difference in mechanical property between the two material.

It has already been stated that deformed α does not recrystallize, but only recover because of strain-induced precipitation of Nb(C, N) in the α substructure, which leads to a fine α-grain structure. The sizable influence on grain refinement of deformation in the two-phase region was observed in Nb-free steel too. Priestner and de los Rios reported that when transformation began during rolling, the much greater refinement of the α-grain size resulted from extra intragranular formation of α-grain, indicating that it was the substructure, and not microalloyed precipitate, that caused the extra nucleation of α . Melloy and Dennison and other investigator attributed grain refinement to the dynamic recovery and/or dynamic recrystallization of α in Nb-free steel.

## Ar3 temperature during controlled rolling

Depending on its purpose, controlled rolling is performed either in the γ-region (austenite region) alone or in the two-phase region. Therefore, to perform controlled rolling adequately, the Ar3 temperature during the controlled-rolling process must be known precisely. In controlled-rolled steel, strain energy stored during deformation in the non-recrystallization region accelerates the γ to α transformation, i.e. a strain-induced transformation takes place, thereby raising the Ar3 temperature. The measurement of strain-induced Ar3 temperature has been performed by a variety of technique, thermal analysis, dilatometric method with compression device, and microstructural change. However, these measurement were not always carried out with precision or under the condition where real controlled rolling was simulated, because of the limitation imposed by instrument and/or the difficulty in simulating controlled rolling. Tanaka and Tabata reported that the strain-induced Ar3 temperature could be determined correctly by measuring texture intensity, which can be applied to any controlled-rolling condition. Their result is shown in Fig. 23, where the Ar3 temperature increase with increasing amount of reduction in the non-recrystallization region, which is more noticeable in the larger prior austenite grain size.

## PROPERTY OF CONTROLLED-ROLLED STEEL

## Anisotropy due to development of texture

When compared in term of the same carbon equivalent, controlled-rolled steel has greater strength than the conventionally hot-rolled type, and it exhibits a lower transition temperature than normalized, or quenched and tempered steel. However, controlled-rolled steel has its own disadvantage. The most serious one is the anisotropy in mechanical property due to texture development.

In controlled-rolled steel a crystallographic texture develops, the magnitude of which depends on whether deformation is carried out in the non-recrystallization region or in the two-phase region, or whether the microstructure consists of α (ferrite) or bainite. Yutori and Ogawa reported that even when deformation in the non-recrystallization region is given under the same rolling condition, the intensity in texture is different depending on transformed microstructure, see Fig. 24. All three structure exhibit a similar texture, consisting of $\langle 110\rangle \| \mathrm{RD}$ (rolling direction) orientation with the strongest component of $\{113\} \langle 110\rangle$ and $\{332\} \langle 113\rangle$. However, there is a remarkable difference in intensity between polygonal ferrite-pearlite and acicular ferrite or martensite. When steel has a low Mn (manganese) and/or Ni content, producing an α-structure, it shows a weak texture intensity. However, with an increasing Mn and/or Ni content the microstructure becomes bainitic, developing a texture with $\{332\} \langle 113\rangle$ and $\{311\} \langle 011\rangle$ orientation.

As shown in Fig. 22, α-phase deformed in the two-phase region remains mainly in the recovered condition in Nb steel. This means that the texture developed by deformation in the two-phase region is the 'cold-rolled' texture. One example of texture developed by deformation in the two-phase region is shown in Fig. 25. Exhibiting ferrite—pearlite structure, the three have basically the same texture, the intensity being raised with an increasing reduction in the two-phase region. A weak texture with $\{112\}\langle 110\rangle$ and $\{554\}\langle 225\rangle$ component develops by heavy deformation in the γ-region (austenite region) alone. Deformation in the two-phase region produced texture consisting of (i) $\langle 110\rangle \|RD$ partial fibre texture, (ii) $\langle 100\rangle \|ND$ texture (ND is normal direction, where the $\langle 100\rangle$ axis is perpendicular to the plate surface), (iii) $\langle 111\rangle \|ND$, and (iv) $\langle 110\rangle \|TD$ (transverse direction) texture with a strong $\{554\}$ $\langle 225\rangle$ component. Among those four texture, (iii) and (iv) do not have a detrimental effect on mechanical property, but (i) causes plane anisotropy and (ii) causes embrittlement in the through-thickness direction. The plane anisotropy in mechanical property caused by the $\langle 110\rangle \|RD$ texture was examined theoretically and experimentally by Inagaki et al., shown in Figs. 26 and 27, where toughness is represented in term of normal stress acting on the cleavage surface, i.e. the $\{100\}$ plane. The diagonal $(45^{\circ})$ direction has low strength but a high susceptibility to cleavage fracture (high transition temperature). The longitudinal $(0^{\circ})$ and transverse $(90^{\circ})$ direction exhibit high strength and low susceptibility to cleavage fracture (low transition temperature). Figure 28 shows plane anisotropy developed in steel finish rolled in the non-recrystallization region or in the two-phase region. The former develops a weak texture, showing indistinct anisotropy, while the latter develops strong plane anisotropy due to an intensive texture, which is very similar to Figs. 26 and 27.

## Separation

In controlled-rolled steel, a matter more serious than plane anisotropy is embrittlement in the through-thickness direction, resulting mainly from the formation of a $\{100\}$ texture. Figure 29 shows schematically the full Charpy curve and number of separation in the L(longitudinal) and Z(through-thickness) direction, where curve of the T(transverse) direction are located near those of the L direction. The difference in transition temperature between the L and Z direction is more than 100 K. The low transition temperature in the L direction is due to separation (very often called delamination or splitting) which occur in a brittle manner in a fractured Charpy speciman parallel to the plate surface. As shown in Fig. 30, separation is greatest near the temperature where the ductile-fracture area becomes just 100%, being nil in the brittle range or at high temperature. In contrast to conventionally hot-rolled steel, the Charpy impact energy of controlled-rolled steel increase with increasing temperature even in the ductile-fraction region, while the number of separation decreases. Impact energy reaches the shelf energy and separation disappears when the temperature reaches the transition temperature in the Z direction.

28 Anisotropies of strength and transition temperature; finish rolled in a non-recrystallization region and b austenite–ferrite region; after Tanaka

29 Schematic representation of full Charpy curve in longitudinal L and through-thickness Z direction of controlled-rolled steel; after Kozasu

The occurrence of separation, accompanied by a lowering of the transition temperature, has been explained in term of the critical stress criterion. When the Charpy speciman is given a bending force the maximum stress are induced at the plastic/elastic interface, just beneath a notch under the plane-strain condition. Induced stress is greatest in the $L$ direction, followed by the $Z$ and $T$ direction, when a longitudinal speciman is considered. The condition for the occurrence of separation is given by

$$
\sigma_ {\mathrm{f}} ^ {\mathrm{L}} > \sigma_ {\mathrm{L}} \quad , \tag{5}
$$

$$
\sigma_ {\mathrm{f}} ^ {\mathrm{Z}} = \sigma_ {\mathrm{Z}} \quad , \tag{6}
$$

where $\sigma_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{L}}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{Z}}$ are the cleavage fracture strength in the $L$ and $Z$ direction, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{Z}}$ are the stress acting in the $L$ and $Z$ direction, respectively. By subtracting (6) from (5), we obtain

30 Occurrence of separation in Nb (niobium) steel deformed in austenite–ferrite region

$$
\sigma_ {\mathrm{f}} ^ {\mathrm{L}} - \sigma_ {\mathrm{f}} ^ {\mathrm{Z}} \geqslant \sigma_ {\mathrm{L}} - \sigma_ {\mathrm{Z}} = k ^ {\prime} \sigma_ {\mathrm{y}} \tag{7}
$$

where $\sigma_{y}$ is the uniaxial yield stress and $k'$ is a constant. As is clear from equation (7), separation occurs only when there is anisotropy in the fracture strength, i.e. only when fracture strength is lower for the Z direction than for the L direction. As the occurrence of separation changes the stress state from plane strain to plane stress, it becomes more difficult for brittle fracture to occur. Embury et al. and Miyoshi et al. reported that separated material behave in a similar manner to that of laminated plate.

The cause of through-thickness embrittlement has been studied by many investigator, and the following suggested: (i) a crack initiates at an MnS inclusion flattened by low-temperature finish rolling, and propagate along grain with $\{100\}$ orientation and/or a banded structure; (ii) the cluster of crystal grain with $\{100\}$ orientation are the main source of separation crack, since separation occurs even in steel with an extremely low S content, and this is strongly supported by the observation that separation increased with increasing intensity in the $\{100\}$ texture; (iii) intergranular failure along prior γ-boundary (austenite boundary), probably embrittled by the segregation of impurity, increases the occurrence of separation; (iv) in hot-rolled strip, temper embrittlement caused by the segregation of P to α-grain (ferrite grain) boundary in the rich layer during slow cooling after coiling deteriorates boundary toughness; (v) dimensional anisotropy of the microstructure produced by controlled rolling — γ-grain in the case of the intergranular fracture, and α-grain in the case of transgranular — is the main cause of through-thickness embrittlement; (vi) pearlite and/or a bainite banded structure; and (vii) a combination of these effect.

The mechanism initiating separation may depend on chemical composition, microstructure, and hot-rolling condition. When stress is induced in the through-thickness direction, crack initiate at the place where the fracture strength is lowest, and propagate along the second weakest location. When flattened MnS exists in steel, it triggers the initiation of the crack, which propagates along grain with $\{100\}$ orientation and/or bainite and/or the pearlite band, depending on the situation. If MnS exists very occasionally in steel with an extremely low S content, separation will initiate at the second weakest location.

Separation has a large effect on transition temperature and absorbed energy. The latter is influenced most markedly near the temperature where shear area becomes just 100%, exhibiting the greatest number of separation. As shown in Fig. 31, both absorbed energy and transition temperature decrease with an increasing number of separation. As is clear from the above explanation, the low-temperature toughness in the L and T direction is improved by the sacrifice of that in the Z direction.

## Elimination of separation

Various method have been proposed to prevent the occurrence of separation. In order to eliminate flattened MnS which triggers the initiation of separation, inclusion-shape control has been employed, which convert elongated sulphide to a globular inclusion by the addition of rare earth metal and/or Ca. Advancing the sulphide-shape control technique, a new desulphurization method has been developed, which can reduce the S content to an extremely low level. Finish rolling in the γ-region result in the formation of a weak $\{100\}$ texture, suppressing markedly the occurrence of separation. A decrease in the P content is desirable, since it causes temper embrittlement during slow cooling after coiling in hot-rolled strip. Once initiated separation has a propensity to propagate along the banded structure. Mori et al. reported that the occurrence of separation is determined by the combined effect of band density and $\{100\}$ intensity, and that the addition of Cr disperses a banded structure, thereby suppressing the occurrence of separation.

## STRENGTHENING AND TOUGHENING MECHANISMS

## Equation describing strength and toughness

The strengthening mechanism in controlled-rolled steel will be described briefly. The yield stress of polycrystalline solid follows the Hall–Petch relation:

$$
\left| \begin{array}{c}\sigma_ {\mathbf {y}} = \sigma_ {\mathbf {o}} + k _ {\mathbf {y}} d ^ {- 1 / 2} \\ = (\sigma_ {\mathrm{lh}} + \sigma_ {\mathrm{sh}} + \sigma_ {\mathrm{dh}} + \sigma_ {\mathrm{ph}}) + k _ {\mathbf {y}} d ^ {- 1 / 2}. \end{array} \right|\tag{8}
$$

where $\sigma_{0}$ is internal stress, d is grain size, and $k_{y}$ is a constant; $\sigma_{0}$ is divided into several term: lattice hardening, solid-solution hardening, dislocation hardening, and precipitation hardening. Observing extra hardening due to texture development, Little et al. and Coleman et al. proposed to add texture hardening $\sigma_{text}$ to equation (8) which was, however, found to be quite small. Baker and McPherson observed strengthening due mainly to subgrain hardening in microstructure mixed with subgrain:

$$
\sigma_ {\mathbf {y}} = \sigma_ {0} + k _ {\mathbf {y}} d ^ {- 1 / 2} + \sigma_ {\mathrm{text}} + \sigma_ {\mathrm{sub}} \tag{9}
$$

Matsuda et al. reported that in the martensitic structure the prior γ-grain (austenite grain) was divided into several block, which play the same role with large-angle grain, becoming obstacle to the propagation of yield and cleavage crack. The concept of this 'effective grain size' was evidenced by other investigator. Equation (8) is rewritten as

$$
\sigma_ {\mathbf {y}} = \sigma_ {0} + k d _ {\mathrm{e}} ^ {- 1 / 2} \tag{10}
$$

where $d_{e}$ is the effective grain size. Deformation in the two-phase region produces a mixed grain structure consisting of polygonal grain and sub-grain or cellular substructure. Bramfitt and Marder proposed that the cell contribution to yield strength could be added by allowing for respective volume fraction of grain and cell in a partially recrystallized structure as follows:

32 Yield strength v. microstructure parameter, which takes into account contribution from both equiaxed grain size and subgrain or cell size; after Bramfitt and Marder

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \sigma_ {\mathbf {y}} = \sigma_ {\mathbf {o}} + k _ {\mathbf {y}} d ^ {- 1 / 2} (1 - f _ {\mathbf {c}}) \\ + k _ {\mathbf {c}} d _ {\mathbf {c}} ^ {- 1 / 2} f _ {\mathbf {c}} \end{array}\tag{11}
$$

where $f_{\mathbf{c}}$ is the fraction of cell structure, and $k_{\mathbf{y}}$ and $k_{\mathbf{c}}$ are the experimentally determined value for plot of fully recrystallized structure and fully cellular structure, respectively. This model gave an approximate fit to the experimental datum, see Fig. 32.

From a theoretical point of view, Heslop and Petch showed that the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature is inversely proportional to $d^{-1/2}$, where d is the grain size. Based on the observation that, in a martensitic structure, the facet unit was the effective grain size, Kunitake et al. gave the transition temperature as

$$
T _ {\mathbf {r s}} = A - B \log d _ {\mathrm{e}} ^ {- 1 / 2} \tag{12}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constant. Gladman et al. gave the transition temperature of bainitic steel by the equation:

$$
\begin{array}{r l} T _ {\mathrm{rs}} (^ {\circ} \mathrm{C}) & = - 19 + 44 (\% \mathrm{Si}) + 700 (\% \mathrm{N} _ {\mathrm{free}}) ^ {1 / 2} \\ & \quad + 0.26 (\sigma_ {\mathrm{D}} + \Delta P + \Delta) - 11.5 d ^ {- 1 / 2} \end{array}\tag{13}
$$

where $\sigma_{\mathrm{D}}$ is Ashby-Orowan strengthening from dispersed second-phase particle, and $\Delta P$ and $\Delta$ are the assumed strengthening contribution from random or forest dislocation and the contribution from dislocation in low-angle boundary, respectively. As is clear from equation (13), all of the strengthening factor raise the transition temperature. The only exception is grain refinement, which increases yield strength and at the same time reduces transition temperature.

33 Effect of finishing temperature on transition temperature and grain size; the former increase rapidly when deformation temperature is lowered to austenite–ferrite region; after Speich and Dabkowski

The sub-boundary cannot be an obstacle to the propagation of brittle cracking. However, if sub-grain form a cluster, thereby developing a high-angle boundary, this can arrest brittle cracking. As shown in Fig. 31, the transition temperature decreases in a linear manner with the number of separation. Taking these effect into consideration, Tanaka proposed the following equation:

$$
\begin{array}{r l} T _ {\mathrm{rs}} = \Delta T + A (\sigma_ {\mathrm{ph}} + \sigma_ {\mathrm{dh}} + \Delta) & \\ - B d ^ {- 1 / 2} (1 - f _ {\mathrm{s}}) - C d _ {\mathrm{e}} ^ {- 1 / 2} f _ {\mathrm{s}} - E n _ {\mathrm{s}} \end{array}\tag{14}
$$

where $\Delta T$ is a constant depending on chemical composition; $A, B, C$, and $E$ are constant; $f_{\mathrm{S}}$ is the volume fraction of subgrain; $d_{\mathrm{e}}$ is the effective grain size, where $d_{\mathrm{e}}$ is in between the equiaxed grain and subgrain size; and $n_{\mathrm{S}}$ is the number of separation.

## Interpretation of mechanical property

The report on variation in transition temperature with deformation temperature in the two-phase region have been in disagreement with each other. As shown in Fig. 33, the transition temperature increased with a decrease in finishing temperature in the two-phase region; it reached a minimum at a certain temperature in the two-phase region, and increased again with a further decrease in finishing temperature. The transition temperature decreased with decreasing deformation temperature; excessive reduction in the two-phase region raised the transition temperature; and heavy reduction in the two-phase region lowered the transition temperature of plain carbon steel. Those contradictory report are explained consistently by equation (14). In steel deformed in the two-phase region, the second term $A(\sigma_{\mathrm{ph}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{dh}} + \Delta)$ and the last term $En_{\mathrm{S}}$ on the right-hand side of equation (14) have a particularly large influence on transition temperature. If the contribution to the transition temperature from the second term, in particular dislocation hardening $\sigma_{\mathrm{dh}}$, is larger than that from separation, the transition temperature increase. On the other hand, if the contribution from separation is larger than that from dislocation hardening, the transition temperature decreases.

When deformed just below the Ar3 temperature, the cellular dislocation structure changes quickly into a subgrain structure, eliminating large dislocation hardening. However, when deformed at lower temperature, insufficient recovery raises $\sigma_{\mathrm{dh}}$, which exceeds the effect of separation and thereby increases the transition temperature. In Nb (niobium) steel, conflict between dislocation hardening and separation is severe because fine precipitate of strain-induced Nb(C, N) pin down dislocation, and thereby retard recovery and recrystallization. On the other hand, in C-Mn steel, dislocation hardening is small owing to the rapid progress of recovery and, at the same time, there is a large effect of separation due to the development of $\{100\}$ texture, which causes a decrease in transition temperature even when finish rolled at low temperature and/or heavily deformed.

## EFFECT OF ALLOYING ELEMENT

Alloying element which enhance strength and toughness are most desirable. There are three way of increasing strength; grain refining, precipitation and/or solid-solution hardening, and transformation hardening. An improvement in toughness is achieved by either grain refining or by toughening the α-matrix (ferrite matrix) itself. Since grain refining enhances both strength and toughness, grain-refining element are most desirable. Grain refinement is attained by fine dispersion of a second phase and/or by lowering the transformation temperature by the addition of substitutional alloying element. Needless to say the purpose of controlled rolling is to achieve grain refinement and thereby to improve mechanical property. The effect of each alloying element is represented in term of its contribution to strength and transition temperature. Besides strength and toughness, weldability is a very important factor, which improves with the decreasing carbon equivalent and, in particular, C content.

The microalloying element, such as Nb and Ti (titanium), are indispensable in controlled-rolled steel. In the early stage of development, Nb was employed mainly for precipitation hardening. However, since Nb was found to improve strength and toughness very effectively through grain refinement, it has become an indispensable element in controlled-rolled steel. The effect of Nb, V, and Ti on strength are shown in Fig. 34. Nb contributes to strength via both grain refining and precipitation; particularly in a low Nb content, major hardening is due to grain refinement. V causes a large increase in both strength and transition temperature through precipitation hardening. Ti causes a slight increase in strength via grain refinement and precipitation hardening. Therefore, only Nb enhances both strength and toughness in controlled-rolled steel. The main cause of grain refinement in Nb steel is that Nb in solution delays γ-recrystallization (austenite recrystallization), thereby raising the recrystallization temperature, extending the non-recrystallization region, and intensifying the effect of controlled rolling. It is also considered that strain-induced precipitate of fine Nb(C,N) prevent α-grain growth during the γ to α transformation.

34 Correlation between alloy content and increase in yield strength as result of grain refinement ( $\Delta\sigma_{G}$ ) and precipitation strengthening ( $\Delta\sigma_{ph}$ ); after Heisterkamp and Meyer

In comparison with Nb, the effect of V on grain refinement is slight. The retarding effect of recrystallization was not observed at low temperature in the γ-region. The addition of Ti slows down grain growth during slab reheating or after the recrystallization of γ. When added in large quantity ($\sim$0.1%), Ti was reported to retard the recrystallization of γ. However, since Ti decreases the toughness of both base steel and the heat-affected-zone of weldment, its use is limited. In general, precipitate formed in γ at high temperature are incoherent, causing little increase in strength. While precipitate formed in the ferrite matrix are coherent and raise the strength and transition temperature rapidly. Hashimoto et al. showed that strain-induced precipitate raise strength, without impairing toughness, because of being incoherent but very fine. Controlled-rolled steel frequently makes combined use of Nb (niobium) and V; Nb aids grain refining and V precipitation hardening.

Substitutional solute atom contribute to the mechanical property of controlled-rolled steel through solid-solution hardening, extension of the temperature range of controlled rolling, and refinement of transformation product owing to the lowering of the transformation temperature. It is worth noting that controlled rolling produces a ferrite grain structure by mean of large deformation in the low-temperature γ-range and accelerating the γ to α (ferrite) transformation in steel with medium hardenability, which will become bainitic in the conventionally hot rolled or normalized condition. Therefore, excessive addition of alloying element will suppress the α-transformation and the formation of a fine-grained ferrite structure, even in controlled-rolled steel.

Si (silicon) exhibits a good strength—ductility relation at 0.3–0.5% in controlled-rolled steel as well as in the normalized type. Manganese is one of the essential element in structural steel because it causes solid-solution hardening and ferrite grain refinement via lowering of the transformation temperature. The effect of Mn (manganese) addition, up to a certain critical content, is to harden steel gradually by mean of solid solution. However, further addition increase yield strength markedly due to transformation hardening. The addition of small amount of Cr, Cu, and/or Ni ($\leqslant$0.3%) has little effect on the property of controlled-rolled steel. These element are effective when used in combination with Nb and/or V, since they promote the formation of very fine precipitate via lowering of the transformation temperature. As already mentioned, Cr suppresses the formation of a band-ed structure, thereby preventing the occurrence of separation. Mo (molybdenum) causes an increase in strength mainly through transformation hardening. Mo is one of the essential element in producing acicular ferrite steel, as referred to below.

## PRACTICE OF CONTROLLED ROLLING IN PRODUCTION MILL

In the production mill, factor governing the controlled-rolling process are inter-related and a variety of approach can be used to attain the same objective. The important factor are as follows: (i) lowering of the slab-reheating temperature to obtain small and uniform γ-grain (austenite grain) size; (ii) γ-grain refinement via recrystallization; (iii) selection of a suitable pass schedule and, in particular, the amount of reduction per pass during the initial pass to obtain a fine and uniform recrystallized γ-grain structure; (iv) selection of temperature and time of delay between the recrystallization region and the non-recrystallization region; and (v) a suitable amount of reduction and rolling temperature in the two-phase region. They are virtually equivalent to and interchangeable with each other, implying that a suitable combination of some of them would suffice to control-roll steel adequately. It is for this reason that the stressing factor differs from one investigator to another and from one mill to another. Taking into consideration the capacity, efficiency, cooling power, and stability of operation, each mill has its own controlled-rolling process.

The plate mill has difficulty in giving a sufficient amount of reduction per pass and, in particular, during the initial several pass of slab rolling. An improper pass schedule leads to mixed grain structure, causing deterioration in toughness. In order to overcome this difficulty, some investigator emphasize extremely large deformation in the non-recrystallization region. On the other hand, owing to a great deal of freedom in selecting the rolling temperature and distribution of reduction among the recrystallization, non-recrystallization, and two-phase region, the plate mill can meet freely a variety of requirement. In the hot-strip mill, the reduction per pass can be more than the critical one required for the completion of recrystallization in each pass, which makes reduction very easy in the recrystallization region, producing a finer and more uniform γ-grain structure than the plate mill. In the strip mill, however, the time and temperature of holding, distribution of reduction among the recrystallization, non-recrystallization, and two-phase region, and selection of the finishing temperature are quite restricted. Thus, the plate mill and hot-strip mill have their advantage and disadvantage. The practice of controlled rolling is described briefly below.

As shown in Fig. 1, controlled rolling in the plate mill is often carried out in term of a 'rough—hold—finish' schedule: rolling pass in the rougher in the rapid-recrystallization region, a delay period, and rolling pass in the finisher. A delay is necessary to allow a specified total deformation to be introduced in the non-recrystallization region. There is a great possibility that during the holding period, recrystallization and subsequent rapid grain growth will take place or partial recrystallization will occur whereby a mixed α-grain (ferrite grain) structure is formed, deteriorating toughness. Care must be taken, therefore, to ensure the required low finishing temperature while preventing rapid grain growth or partial recrystallization during holding.

Instead of the rough—hold—finish schedule, Jones and Rothwell adopted a 'continuous' schedule involving reduction in the whole range, which produces a uniform, fine-grained structure. Figure 35 depicts the new rolling schedule, i.e. the three-stage rolling process as well as the standard two-stage process (rough—hold—finish), employed by USINOR, Dunkirk. During the delay time at high temperature in the standard two-stage process, recrystallization is rapid even in Nb (niobium) steel, leading to a coarse-grained structure at the end of the delay time. In the three-stage process, the first delay time at high temperature leads to a coarse-grained structure. During the second delay time, recrystallization is sluggish so that the grain size at the end of rolling is finer for the three-stage process than for the second stage.

At the British Steel Corporation, General Steels Division, to minimize recrystallization and grain growth during the delay period, the temperature at the commencement of the delay period is reduced by reducing the reheating temperature.

The temperature at the end of the delay period is controlled in order to allow a specific total deformation to be introduced without inducing an excessively high mill loading. Finish rolling at temperature in the two-phase and/or α-region is employed to increase strength. Total rolling deformation in the non-recrystallization region after the delay period is very important in order to achieve a uniform, fine-grained structure. To fulfil this requirement, the thickness of material at the commencement of re-rolling after the delay period is controlled at either three time or five time that of the final thickness.

Controlled rolling in the hot-strip mill is very different from that in the plate mill: (i) rapid cooling on the run-out table after finish rolling is followed by slow cooling after coiling; (ii) both the rougher and finisher can carry out heavy reduction — during rolling in the finisher, the interpass time is very short, total rolling deformation in the finisher becoming almost one-pass reduction; (iii) rolling temperature and total reduction in the finisher encounter much restriction; (iv) rougher rolling can be regarded as deformation in the recrystallization region, and finisher rolling as deformation in the non-recrystallization region — the total reduction is overwhelmingly larger for rougher rolling than for finisher rolling and reduction per pass is large, which is suitable for achieving fine-grained γ (austenite) through repeated recrystallization, resulting in a uniform, fine-grained α-structure; and (v) during holding at the coiling temperature, precipitation of Nb and V proceed causing a large increase in yield strength. Rolling in the two-phase region is not always carried out, causing few separation. Because of large precipitation hardening and few separation, the transition temperature is usually much higher for hot-rolled strip than for plate. One example of a rolling schedule is shown in Fig. 36. By employing a low slab-reheating temperature and a heavy reduction in the rougher, they obtained a uniform, fine-grained structure, even though the total reduction in the finisher (in the non-recrystallization region) was about 50%.

## ENLARGEMENT OF CONTROLLED-ROLLING PROCESS

As controlled rolling is known to be very useful, it has been applied to various field and its application is being expanded.

## Acicular ferrite steel

Acicular ferrite, HSLA (high-strength low-alloy) steel has been developed by the Climax Molybdenum Company. Low-carbon ($\leqslant$0.06%) Mn (manganese)–Mo (molybdenum)–Nb (niobium) steel which will transform to upper bainite from undeformed or conventionally hot-rolled γ, transforms to acicular ferrite, when transformation is accelerated by controlled rolling. Figure 37 shows the acicular ferrite structure (Fig. 37a) as well as the bainitic structure (Fig. 37b). The acicular ferrite structure consists of fine non-equiaxed ferrite dispersed with cementite and martensite island.

The acicular ferrite is defined as a highly substructured, non-equiaxed phase that forms on continuous cooling by a mixed diffusion and shear mode of transformation at a temperature slightly higher than the upper bainite transformation range. Acicular ferrite is different from bainitic ferrite with respect to the prior γ-grain-boundary network and cementite and martensite morphology; in the bainitic structure, the prior γ-boundary network is retained and plate-like cementite are formed at coarse lath boundary as well as the prior grain boundary, whereas in the acicular ferrite structure the prior γ-grain-boundary network is completely eliminated having a fine-grained structure, and small cementite and martensite island are scattered throughout the matrix (see Fig. 37). Because of the above difference in microstructure between bainitic and acicular ferrite there is a distinct difference in the facet unit (effective grain size) which, in turn, causes a large difference in transition temperature between the two. In the bainitic structure, a facet unit is nearly equal to the prior γ-grain size, whereas in the acicular ferrite a facet unit is much smaller than the prior γ-grain size, giving a low transition temperature.

The fully acicular ferrite which, being free of polygonal ferrite, contains a small amount of cementite and martensite, exhibits high strength but poor toughness. A significant improvement in toughness can be obtained in the mixed structure of acicular plus fine-grained polygonal ferrite by lowering the finish-rolling temperature and by increasing the amount of deformation in the non-recrystallization region. The reason for the improvement is grain refinement in the polygonal ferrite as well as acicular ferrite. As shown in Fig. 38, with the increase in the amount of deformation in the non-recrystallization region, fine-grained polygonal ferrite increase in volume fraction at the expense of acicular ferrite which, in turn, causes an improvement in strength and low-temperature toughness. The optimum combination of strength and toughness is obtained with ~15% of polygonal ferrite. On the other hand, the introduction of coarse polygonal ferrite to acicular ferrite causes a deterioration in strength property as well as impact property. Cause of coarse polygonal-ferrite formation are insufficient hardenability and inadequate controlled rolling in term of finish-rolling temperature, and the amount of deformation in the non-recrystallization region.

## As-hot-rolled dual-phase steel

Dual-phase steel has a microstructure consisting of α-grain (ferrite grain) dispersed with fine martensite island. It is characterized by continuous yielding followed by rapid work hardening, which results in a low yield but high tensile strength and large elongation. Dual-phase steel can be produced in the as-hot-rolled condition by the combination of suitable chemical composition and rolling condition. When steel containing both strong ferrite former like Si (silicon) and transformation-delaying element such as Cr, Mn (manganese), and/or Mo (molybdenum) is cooled after hot rolling, the microstructure consists of α - and γ-phase (austenite phase). The latter is stabilized due to carbon enrichment and thereby transforms to martensite at low temperature. When deformation is applied in the non-recrystallization region, strain-assisted γ to α transformation occurs, thereby raising the α-transformation temperature on one hand and reducing the martensite transformation temperature on the other, which makes it easy to produce ferrite plus martensite dual-phase steel.

## Controlled rolling of C-Mn steel

Gohda et al. and Hashimoto et al. reported that when deformed in the two-phase region, Nb-free (niobium free) steel exhibit improvement in strength and toughness and, further, that heavy deformation in the two-phase region does not deteriorate toughness. Increase in strength by deformation in the two-phase region is due to either subgrain formation in the recovery region or dislocation hardening in the non-recovery region. The ease of recovery and occurrence of separation are responsible for good toughness of steel obtained by heavy deformation in the two-phase region. The effect of deformation in the two-phase region is essentially the same between Nb-bearing and Nb-free steel. The difference lies in the ease of recovery, which causes difference in the optimum condition of finishing temperature and/or strain. Controlled-rolled C—Mn steel has started to be used as material for low-temperature service.

## Controlled rolling as pretreatment

By making use of grain-refining effect, controlled rolling is employed as a pretreatment before normalizing or quenching and tempering. This is based on the fact that a fine-grained structure produced by controlled rolling persist even in the reheated condition, probably due to the dispersion of fine Nb(C, N) precipitate. In Nb and 3.5%Ni steel, controlled rolling plus normalizing produces higher strength and better toughness than normalizing alone.

Linepipe steel for Arctic use is usually produced by controlled rolling. However, when the thickness is increased too much the controlled-rolling effect cannot be exerted over the whole thickness. Controlled rolling plus quenching and tempering produces much tougher material than the single process alone. The fine γ-grain size before quenching is responsible for this. Controlled rolling plus controlled cooling and controlled rolling followed by direct quenching have been tried.

A new type of thermomechanical treatment has been proposed by Miyoshi et al. After controlled rolling, C-Mn and Nb steel are cooled below the Ar1 temperature and subsequently heated to ~900 °C, which produces a very fine-grained γ-structure owing to the superimposed effect of controlled rolling, transformation, and normalizing. Fine-grained γ is once again controlled rolled, producing an extremely fine and uniform α-grain (ferrite grain) structure.
